newsitem.title: CONGO: Zaire's elite flee capital in steady trickle.
newsitem.headline: Zaire's elite flee capital in steady trickle.

text.p: A steady trickle of President Mobutu Sese Seko's entourage have been fleeing the sprawling Zairean capital, fearing retribution from advancing rebels and a potentially bitter end to his three-decade rule.

On Friday, speed boats, one carrying televisions, lamps and even furniture, zipped accross the vast Zaire river which divides the twin capitals of Kinshasa and Brazzaville, landing at a private beech.
Mercedes Benz and Jaguar cars with Kinshasa number plates cruise the streets of the Congolese capital, and even one government-owned Daewoo has found its way across the river.
Congolese immigration officials say that many of the Zaireans who have left because of their close connections to Mobutu have flown on to other destinations.
"They come to Brazzaville after crossing the river but the wealthier ones travel on by plane to the four corners of the world," a senior security official at the port told Reuters.
The Zairean Minister of Youth and Sports, Kisombe Kiaku Mwisi, attempted a discreet departure on the Sabena flight to Brussels on Friday.
Kisombe, who is also a senior member of Mobutu's Popular Revolutionary Movement MPR declined a place in the VIP lounge after being identified by Congolese airport officials.

He preferred to remain amongst the other passengers, and declined comment to reporters at the airport. Another senior member of the beleaguered cabinet sent his family off from Brazzaville by plane on Friday, hotel workers said.
Mobutu himself flew out of Kinshasa on Friday morning bound for his jungle palace at Gbadolite in the north of Zaire. An official broadcast said his doctors had advised him to take a few days rest.

For the ailing president, who is battling with prostate cancer as well as the final thrust of Laurent Kabila's seven-month-old rebellion, France and Morocco, where he has properties, and even South Africa, have offered him sanctuary, should he decide to leave the country.
Access to foreign destinations for many other Zaireans who may not trust the intentions of Kabila, whose forces are poised to capture Kinshasa, is not so easy.
"The big problem is getting visas to go on. Look at me I've got my daughter in France but they won't give me a visa to see her and my grandchildren," a senior Zairean diplomat in Brazzaville said.
The diplomat said it was impossible to tell how many Zaireans had fled to Congo in the past few weeks because there are numerous private beaches and crossings on the river frontier.
Those who have made it out in time now worry about the fate of those left behind.
"They could have come yesterday but they refused. Now we're worried," said a young man from Mobutu's extended family, sitting in the lobby of a Brazzaville hotel.
Embassies, U.N. agencies and some expatriate businessmen have steadily reduced their staff as the rebels approached the Zairean capital.
Some ordinary inhabitants of Kinshasa have sent their children over to Congo to stay with relatives until the situation stabilizes.

"I am just here to take my two sons to stay with their aunt for their security. But I myself will go back tommorrow. I trust that God will bring peace to Kinshasa," said Marie Jose, an inhabitant of the working class Kasavubu district of Kinshasa.
The vast majority of Kinshasa's five million inhabitants have stayed behind.
